title: Issue-triage agent with a 30-case eval
summary: Build an agent that does a maintainer's first look at a new issue: label it, spot a duplicate, list what is missing, draft a reply. Then prove how well it works on 30 cases you labelled yourself.
context: Maintainers of busy open-source projects lose hours to the first look at each new issue: is it a bug, a question or a feature request, has it been reported, can anyone reproduce it from what is written.

Invent a small open-source project (say, a fictional command-line tool) and generate or hand-write at least 100 fictional issues for it, with fictional authors. Include duplicates, vague reports, questions posted as bugs, and an issue with an empty body.
The agent is the smaller half of the job. The larger half is an eval you cannot flatter: 30 cases, labelled by you before you run anything.
must_have: A triage function: given an issue it returns one label from a set you define, a duplicate verdict naming the earlier issue or none, what is missing to reproduce it, and a drafted first reply that is never posted anywhere.
An eval set of exactly 30 hand-labelled cases covering every label, at least five duplicate pairs, and several tricky ones.
An eval script that prints per-label precision and recall, duplicate accuracy, and every wrong answer with its input.
A baseline that uses no model (keywords or TF-IDF) scored on the same 30, so the agent's gain is a number.
Your committed scores and a short account of the failure cases you found and what you did, or chose not to do, about each.
nice_to_have: A rubric of three or four yes/no questions applied by you to ten drafted replies.
A mode that reads open issues from a real public repo through the unauthenticated GitHub API; nothing from it is committed.
A confidence value you show to be roughly calibrated.
constraints: No paid services, APIs or accounts. Use a small local model or a free tier that needs no card, and commit recorded model outputs so a reader can reproduce your scores without a key.
Fictional data only. Do not copy real people's issue text or usernames into the repo.
The agent drafts only: it never posts, labels or comments on anything.
deliverables: A public repo created after you press Start, with commits spread across the window.
A README with how to run the triage, run the eval, re-record model outputs, your current scores, and what is missing.
judge_focus: Whether the eval could have failed the agent, and how you kept yourself from labelling to fit its output.
What you changed because of a failure case, and what you left alone on purpose.
A trail of commits: the eval set and the baseline before the agent, then each change justified by a failure.
Your account of what AI produced, what you checked, and what you threw away.
bengaluru_context: Developer-tools and open-source program teams at Bengaluru product companies build triage assistants like this, and are asked how they measure one before trusting it.
